Long-term single-family rental investments

I buy rental properties for my family. I help other investors buy the same way.

I buy mostly brand-new single-family rentals in growing markets across the South and Southeast. When I work with investors, I help them buy from the same builders, in the same areas, and using the same criteria I use for my family’s investments.

I focus on the Sun Belt because that is where I consistently find the strongest rental investment opportunities. In high-cost markets like New Jersey, New York and California, purchase prices, property taxes and HOA or condo costs can make it difficult for rent to cover the cost of owning the property, leaving the investor more dependent on future appreciation. In the markets I target, the relationship between purchase price, rent and ongoing costs can be far more favorable, giving the property a much better chance to produce income while also building equity and benefiting from long-term appreciation. The real work is identifying which specific markets, communities and properties are actually worth buying.

I’ve already spent years figuring out what to look for. You don’t have to repeat that journey or turn real estate into a second job.

Why I invest this way

I built this approach for my own family first.

The common thread in my investing has always been to buy carefully first rather than hope to fix a bad decision later.

My first real-estate investments were two luxury homes I bought through sheriff auctions near my home. Both were very profitable, and neither needed much renovation. The returns came mainly from researching them carefully and buying them at the right price.

After COVID, far fewer worthwhile properties were making it to auction, so I started looking at other ways to invest in real estate. A friend introduced me to long-term rentals out of state, and I eventually bought my first one in Alabama.

I was nervous. It was a lot of money, far from home, and completely new territory. I paid far too much to buy down the mortgage rate because I wanted the monthly numbers to feel as safe as possible.

As I bought more, I saw rent estimates I didn’t believe, management I wasn’t comfortable with, and properties recommended without enough attention to the lot, rental competition or what was being built nearby. So I started checking more myself.

Over time I began working directly with builders, got my real-estate licenses, managed my own properties and learned the leasing side firsthand. Once I had a process I trusted, friends started asking me to help them buy similar properties. Then friends of friends started calling.

The process I use with investors is essentially the process I built for my own family.

04
POSSIBLE TAX BENEFIT

Taxes

Rental property typically creates tax benefits. Since they vary so widely, I do not estimate taxes in investment projections. The eventual tax result can also depend on what you choose after a long-term hold—for example, selling, exchanging into another property, or refinancing.

Some sources estimate that the average savings on taxes compared to stock investments are equivalent to around 1.2% in returns on investment per year

HOW I HANDLE IT

How I screen properties
Before I recommend a property, I try to answer four questions.
See what I checkHide checks

Is the rent realistic?

I compare multiple sources rather than relying on a single rent estimate. Because I own properties in the same areas, I also have ongoing, first-hand contact with leasing activity and actual rents, which gives me a very good grasp of what rent is realistic.

How much competition is coming?

I keep an eye on future supply and pay close attention to what other investors are buying, how much similar inventory is being added, and how quickly it is reaching the rental market.

Is something permanently wrong?

A bad lot cannot be renovated later. Grade, usable backyard, road exposure, privacy and future neighboring construction can matter as much as the floor plan.

Are the financing terms actually good?

Builder incentives, closing-cost assistance and mortgage-rate options can materially change the investment.

My rule is simple: if I wouldn’t buy it for my own family, I don’t recommend it to someone else.Sometimes that means I finish the research and decide there is nothing I’m willing to recommend right now.

Cash flow
i
What it means

The top number is the estimated cash left each month after the recurring expenses included in this model.

The bottom number converts that monthly cash flow into an annual cash-on-cash return based on Total Invested.

Already deducted
  • Mortgage principal and interest
  • Property taxes
  • Insurance
  • HOA, when applicable
  • A 10% property-management fee
  • The vacancy allowance already reflected in Rent (avg)
Not included
  • Leasing or tenant-placement fees
  • Repairs
  • Tenant-turnover expenses
  • Future capital-replacement reserves

All properties shown here are new construction, so early repair exposure is lower and most issues are covered by a builder warranty. Repairs are nevertheless not included in the cash-flow calculation.

Principal
i
What it means

The top number is the portion of the monthly mortgage payment that pays down loan principal.

That money does not go into your bank account like cash flow does. Instead, it reduces the mortgage balance and increases your equity in the property.

The bottom number shows that annual principal paydown as a percentage of Total Invested so it can be compared with the other return components.

The amount of principal paid each month comes from the property’s mortgage amortization schedule and changes over time.

Calculation

Principal return contribution = monthly principal paid × 12 ÷ total invested

Fit

Who this approach tends to fit.

✓
A GOOD FIT

Long-term investors

You are building wealth over at least seven years, want real estate as part of a diversified portfolio, and are comfortable with modest early cash flow when the overall investment makes sense. Most prefer not to manage the property themselves.

⚖
THE TRADEOFF

Less instant upside. Fewer unknowns.

Brand-new construction usually does not come with instant equity gains. I accept that tradeoff for fewer repair surprises, fewer moving parts, often lower upfront deal costs when builders contribute toward closing or financing costs, and a shorter path from closing to a rent-ready property.

×
PROBABLY NOT A FIT

If you need speed or liquidity

I would be cautious if you may need the invested money back soon, depend on monthly rent for essential living expenses, or want a quick flip or immediate equity gain.

I currently own 12 rental properties using the same general approach I use with investors.

Before real estate became a significant part of my work, I spent years in high tech and earned an MBA. That background probably explains some of my tendency to question assumptions, compare options and want to understand why the numbers work.

I manage my own rental properties, which has taught me a lot about the ownership and leasing side. I do not manage properties for investors.
